content: The Great Plague of Marseille was one of the most devastating outbreaks of bubonic plague in Europe during the early 18th century. The disease arrived in Marseille, France, in 1720 and resulted in the deaths of approximately 100,000 people in the city and surrounding provinces. Despite the catastrophic loss of life, Marseille managed to recover relatively quickly. Economic activity rebounded within a few years, driven by expanding trade with the West Indies and Latin America. By 1765, the population of Marseille had returned to its pre-1720 levels. This epidemic was not a resurgence of the European Black Death, which had ravaged the continent beginning in the 14th century. Instead, the plague bacillus Yersinia pestis was introduced to Marseille in 1720 via a merchant ship arriving from Syria. The ship, which had known cases of plague onboard, was initially placed under quarantine by port authorities. However, due to the city's lucrative trade monopoly with the Levant and the pressing need for the ship's cargo of silk and cotton for the Beaucaire fair, powerful merchants pressured authorities to lift the quarantine. Shortly thereafter, the disease began to spread within the city. Hospitals were quickly overwhelmed as the number of cases surged. Panic ensued among the population, leading to the expulsion of the sick from their homes and the city itself. Mass graves were dug to accommodate the dead, but these quickly filled. Eventually, the sheer number of fatalities overwhelmed public health efforts, leaving thousands of corpses scattered or piled throughout the city. In an attempt to contain the spread of the plague, the Parliament of Aix enacted a law imposing the death penalty for any communication between Marseille and the rest of Provence. To enforce this isolation, a plague wall (Mur de la Peste) was constructed across the countryside. This wall, made of dry stone, stood 2 meters high and 70 centimeters thick, with guard posts positioned along its length. Remnants of this wall can still be seen today in parts of the Plateau de Vaucluse. Over the course of two years, the plague claimed the lives of 50,000 of Marseille's 90,000 residents. An additional 50,000 people died as the disease spread northward, reaching cities such as Aix-en-Provence, Arles, Apt, and Toulon. Mortality rates varied, with Marseille experiencing a death rate of 40%, Toulon exceeding 50%, and Aix and Arles suffering rates of approximately 25%. In 1998, researchers from the Université de la Méditerranée conducted an excavation of a mass grave containing victims of the 1720 plague outbreak. This grave, located in the second district of Marseille at the Monastery of the Observance, provided an opportunity to study over 200 skeletons. Modern laboratory testing, combined with archival research, allowed scholars to uncover new insights into the conditions and timeline of the epidemic. Among the findings was the first historical evidence of an autopsy. The reconstructed skull of a 15-year-old boy revealed that an autopsy had been performed on him during the spring of 1722. The anatomical techniques used in this procedure were consistent with those described in a surgical text from 1708.
